title: Deceptive AI claims and consumer protection

sources.claim: FTC "Operation AI Comply" (September 25, 2024): five actions under existing consumer-protection law, including a company sold as a "robot lawyer" whose claims were alleged to be untested, a tool alleged to generate fake reviews, and schemes promising quick earnings from AI-powered online stores. On December 22, 2025 the FTC reopened and set aside the Rytr (review-tool) order; publishing fake reviews remains deceptive.

sections.skill: Recognize deceptive AI claims and fake reviews as consumer-protection issues

questions.prompt: Do consumer-protection laws apply to AI products?

choices.text: No, because AI is a new technology that existing consumer laws were never written to cover

questions.intro: Consumer-protection laws forbid DECEPTIVE claims, and they apply to AI products too. In September 2024, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced "Operation AI Comply": five actions under EXISTING law, including against a company marketing a "robot lawyer" whose claims were alleged to be untested, a tool alleged to help generate FAKE REVIEWS (that order was set aside in December 2025), and schemes promising quick earnings from AI-powered online stores. Two lessons: claims about what AI can do must be truthful and supported, and publishing fake reviews is deceptive whether a person or a tool wrote them.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: Which claim most needs evidence?
questions.intro: Look for unsupported claims ("our AI is 100% accurate," "replaces your doctor"), hidden limits, and reviews that seem generated or paid without disclosure. The same rules apply whether a person or a tool wrote the claim. Businesses using AI to write marketing remain responsible for checking it. Consumers can report suspected deception to consumer-protection agencies, which use reports to find patterns.
